x: Monize is a self-hosted, web-based personal finance management application. It provides a full suite of tools for tracking your income, expenses, investments, and net worth -- all from a modern, responsive web interface that works as well on a phone as on a desktop, in the language and number format you prefer.

Accounts and transactions Multi-Account Support -- Track chequing, savings, credit cards, loans, mortgages, lines of credit, investments, cash, and assets. See Accounts Transactions -- Splits, transfers, tags, attachments, reconciliation, an advanced search ( payee:costco -cat:gas , amount:50..100 ), columns you can sort and hide, and a month calendar view with daily balances and day notes. See Transactions Attachments and Document Scanning -- Attach receipts and statements to transactions, scan a paper receipt with your phone's camera, and preview files without downloading them Transaction Rules -- Fill in the category, payee, description and tags automatically as transactions arrive, split a row or turn it into a transfer, or send it to the AI review inbox Recurring Transactions -- Schedule bills, deposits, and transfers with flexible recurrence options and a cash flow forecast. See Bills and Deposits Loans and Mortgages -- Annuity, Canadian fixed-rate, linear and interest-only mortgages, rate history, amortization schedules, overpayment scenarios, and bank debits that settle an installment directly Categories, Payees and Tags -- A category hierarchy, payees with contact details and an optional lookup, and flexible cross-category tags (e.g., "Vacation 2026", "Tax Deductible"). This guide walks you through setting up Monize and getting your financial data organized.
Before installing Monize, ensure you have: Docker and Docker Compose installed on your server A minimum of 1 GB RAM available A modern web browser (Chrome, Firefox, Safari, or Edge)

Clone the repository (or download docker-compose.prod.yml and .env.example from it): git clone https://github.com/kenlasko/monize.git cd monize Create your .env file by copying the bundled example: cp .env.example .env The repository ships a .env.example that documents every setting Monize supports, grouped into sections and with the defaults and explanatory comments inline. Anything you do not need can be left commented out -- you do not have to hunt for settings elsewhere. The sections are: Section What it covers Database PostgreSQL connection, TLS, and the optional Row-Level Security roles Application JWT_SECRET , ENCRYPTION_KEY , and general app settings URLs & Ports Host port mappings and the public address of the app ( PUBLIC_APP_URL ) Authentication Local login and registration toggles OIDC / OpenID Connect Single sign-on provider configuration (optional) Bank Sync Diagnostics Extra logging for the Open Banking connection (optional) Email Notifications SMTP server settings (optional) Demo Mode Demo restrictions and the daily reset (optional) MCP / OAuth Debug Logging Extra diagnostics for MCP and OAuth (optional) AI Integration Anthropic, OpenAI, and Ollama settings (optional), including the Email receipts settings: mailbox polling limits, the private-host allowlist, and Google / Microsoft 365 sign-in (see Email Receipts ) Attachments Transaction attachment storage: database, local filesystem, or S3 Backup Backup directory, scheduling, and off-site copies Quote Providers Investment price/quote sources Exchange Rate Providers Where exchange rates come from Update Checks New-version notifications Microsoft Money (.mny) Import The largest Money file that can be uploaded (see Importing from Microsoft Money ) Frontend Local development only At minimum, set JWT_SECRET , ENCRYPTION_KEY and a database password before starting: # Required -- both ship empty, and the server will not start until they are set JWT_SECRET=your-secret-key-minimum-32-characters-long ENCRYPTION_KEY=your-encryption-key-minimum-32-characters # Database (the example file's values) POSTGRES_DB=monize POSTGRES_USER=monize_user POSTGRES_PASSWORD=your-database-password Important Both keys must be at least 32 characters long, and the server refuses to start without either of them. Generate them with openssl rand -base64 32 and openssl rand -hex 32 . A published placeholder or an obviously typed JWT_SECRET still starts, but is logged as a warning and shown to administrators until you replace it. Caution Set ENCRYPTION_KEY , keep it safe, and never change it. It encrypts what Monize stores in the database: AI provider API keys, emergency-access credentials, the key your automatic backups are encrypted with, and the browser-push and OIDC signing keys. Changing or losing it later does not re-encrypt anything -- it makes what is already stored unreadable, and automatic backups stop until every user signs in again. Store it wherever you keep your other deployment secrets, and back it up. ( Backup and Restore has the full picture of what depends on it.) Upgrading from a version where this setting was called AI_ENCRYPTION_KEY ? The old name is still accepted (and wins if both are set), so an existing deployment keeps working untouched. Set ENCRYPTION_KEY to the same value if you want to move to the new name. Likewise, changing JWT_SECRET later signs everyone out, stops authenticator (two-factor) codes from working and forgets trusted devices. Start the application with the prebuilt images: docker compose -f docker-compose.prod.yml up -d The -f is required: the repository has no default Compose file. To build the images from source instead (for development), use docker-compose.dev.yml . Open Monize at http://localhost:3001 (the FRONTEND_PORT and PUBLIC_APP_URL settings in .env ). If you reach it through a reverse proxy or another host name, set PUBLIC_APP_URL to that address.
Helm charts are provided in the helm/ directory for Kubernetes deployments. Refer to the Helm README for detailed configuration options.

Monize publishes prebuilt images to the GitHub Container Registry ( ghcr.io/kenlasko/monize-backend and ghcr.io/kenlasko/monize-frontend ). To update, pull the new images and recreate the containers: docker compose -f docker-compose.prod.yml pull docker compose -f docker-compose.prod.yml up -d Use whichever compose file you started Monize with. up -d only recreates the services whose image changed, and your data stays in the postgres volume. Database migrations run automatically. The backend applies any pending migrations each time it starts, so there is no separate upgrade step. Back up first. Take a backup before updating (see Backup and Restore ), especially across several versions. Pinned tags. If you pin an image tag instead of latest , edit the tag in your compose file before running pull . Clean up. Run docker image prune to remove the old, unused images.

When you first open Monize, you see the sign-in page. Click create a new account under the title Enter your Email address , First name , Last name , Password and Confirm password . The password must be at least 12 characters and contain an uppercase letter, a lowercase letter, a number and a special character Click Create account Important The first account registered on a new server becomes its administrator. Register your own account before you share the address with anyone else. The administrator sees an extra Admin menu (see Settings and Security ). What happens next depends on how the server is set up: Email verification. When the server can send email (SMTP is configured), every account after the first is sent a verification link instead of being signed in. The Check your email screen offers Resend verification email ; click the link in the email, then sign in. Single sign-on. When OIDC is configured, the page also offers Sign up with SSO , and an administrator can turn off local registration altogether, in which case the link does not appear. Once your account is created, two short screens follow before the dashboard: Secure Your Account offers to set up two-factor authentication: re-enter your password, scan the QR code with an authenticator app, and enter its 6-digit code. Click Skip for now to do it later from Settings > Security . If the administrator requires two-factor authentication, there is no skip button. Set Your Preferences asks for the Language of the interface and your Default currency . Click Continue to save them, or Skip for now to keep the defaults. Both can be changed later in Settings. You then land on the dashboard. Until you dismiss it, a Getting Started card at the top links to the first things to set up -- your settings, your categories, your first account, and an import -- and Take the tour starts a short guided introduction to the app. Every guided tour can be started again later from Settings > Guided Tours .

Your default currency is the primary currency used for reporting and net worth calculations. If you skipped it during registration, or want to change it, click Settings (the gear icon with your name in the top-right corner), then choose Default Currency under Preferences > Language & Region . The same section holds the language, theme, date and number formats, and timezone.

A new account starts with no categories. Open Tools > Categories and click Import Default Categories to start from a ready-made set of income and expense categories: pick your Country to also get its tax and benefit categories, and the Language the names are created in. Or click Create Your Own to build the list yourself. See Categories and Payees for the details. If you are about to import from Quicken or Microsoft Money, you can skip this: the import creates the categories your file uses.

Navigate to Accounts from the top navigation bar Click + New Account Fill in the account details: Account Name -- A descriptive name (e.g., "Main Chequing") Account Type -- Chequing, Savings, Credit Card, Investment, Loan, Line of Credit, Mortgage, Asset, Cash or Other (see Accounts for details) Currency -- The currency this account operates in Opening Balance -- The balance the account starts from, before any transaction you record or import Optional details: the account number, the Institution , a credit limit, an interest rate, a foreign currency conversion fee and a description, plus Add to favourites and Exclude from Net Worth . Some types ask for more, such as a credit card's statement dates or a loan's terms Click Create Account An Investment account is created as a linked pair by default: a cash account for money moving in and out, and a brokerage account for the securities (see Investments ). If you already have your history in another program or in your bank's downloads, you can create accounts as part of an import instead -- see Importing Transactions .
The bar at the top of every page gives access to all major features. Click the Monize logo to return to the dashboard.

Menu Item Description Transactions View, search, and manage all transactions Bills & Deposits Manage scheduled and recurring transactions Investments Track your investment portfolio Accounts Manage your accounts and view balances Budgets Plan and track spending against budgets Reports Access built-in and custom reports AI A menu with Insights , the AI Assistant and the AI Review Inbox (see AI )

Click the Tools dropdown to access additional features: Tool Description Payees Manage payee records, aliases and default categories Categories Manage income and expense categories Securities Manage investment securities Currencies View and manage currencies and exchange rates Institutions The banks and brokerages your accounts belong to Tags Manage transaction tags for flexible labelling Warranties Track warranties, their receipts and their claims (see Warranties ) Taxes Payroll deduction rules with yearly maximums. See Taxes Rules Fill in categories, payees and tags automatically when a transaction is created or imported. See Rules Email Receipts Turn order confirmations from a mailbox into itemized transactions (see Email Receipts ) Import Transactions Import CSV, OFX/QFX and QIF files, or a whole Microsoft Money file
The instance administrator also sees an Admin menu with User Management , Notification Settings and Backups (see Settings and Security ).

The right-hand side of the bar holds: Search -- Search your transactions from anywhere Action History -- Your recent changes, with Undo and Redo Notifications -- The bell, with a count of unread notifications Settings -- The gear icon with your first name: preferences, security, two-factor authentication, trusted devices, sharing, backups and more Logout -- Sign out of the application On a phone, the menus move into a drawer opened with the menu button at the top left.

h: Installing as a Progressive Web App
x: Monize is a Progressive Web App (PWA) , which means it can be installed directly from your browser and launched like a native application -- no app store required.

Standalone window -- Monize opens in its own window without browser tabs, address bar, or other browser chrome, giving it a native app feel Home screen / app launcher icon -- Launch Monize with a single tap or click, just like any other installed app Faster startup -- Static assets (JavaScript, stylesheets, fonts, images) are cached locally by the service worker, so the app shell loads quickly on subsequent visits Works on any modern device -- Desktop (Windows, macOS, Linux) and mobile (Android, iOS / iPadOS) Note: The PWA caches the app itself, but your financial data still requires a network connection to your Monize server. The PWA does not provide fully offline access to transactions, accounts, or reports.

Monize must be accessed over HTTPS (or over http://localhost for local development). Browsers will not offer installation on plain HTTP URLs. Use a modern browser that supports PWAs (Chrome, Edge, Safari, Firefox, Brave, Opera, or Samsung Internet).

Open Monize in your browser and sign in Look for the install icon in the address bar (a small monitor or computer icon, often on the right-hand side) Click the icon, then click Install Monize will open in its own window and an icon will be added to your applications list, Start menu, or Dock Alternatively, open the browser menu (three dots) and choose Install Monize... or Apps > Install this site as an app .

h: Installing on Android (Chrome, Edge, Samsung Internet)
x: Open Monize in your mobile browser and sign in Tap the menu button (three dots in the top-right corner) Tap Install app or Add to Home screen Confirm by tapping Install The Monize icon will appear on your home screen and app drawer

Safari does not show an automatic install prompt, so you need to add Monize from the Share menu: Open Monize in Safari (other iOS browsers do not support PWA installation) Tap the Share button (the square with an upward arrow) at the bottom of the screen Scroll down and tap Add to Home Screen Edit the name if desired, then tap Add The Monize icon will appear on your home screen
Open Monize in Firefox and sign in Tap the menu button (three dots) Tap Install or Add to Home screen Confirm the installation

Once installed, Monize appears in the operating system's share sheet on Android and in desktop Chromium browsers (Safari on iPhone and iPad does not support this). Share a receipt or a bank download to Monize and a Shared with Monize screen lists every file it received, with the reason beside any it cannot use, and offers what to do with them: Attach to a new transaction -- for images and PDFs Import as a statement -- for CSV, OFX, QFX and QIF files; this opens the import wizard with the files already loaded (see Importing Transactions ) Send to AI Assistant -- when an AI provider is set up Discard Nothing is saved until you choose. Shared files wait on the device for an hour, and Monize must have been opened on the device at least once before the share sheet can hand it files.

To remove the installed PWA: Desktop -- Open the installed Monize window, click the three-dot menu inside it, and choose Uninstall Monize... . On Windows and macOS you can also uninstall from the operating system's usual apps list. Android -- Long-press the Monize icon and tap Uninstall (or drag it to the uninstall zone) iOS / iPadOS -- Long-press the Monize icon on the home screen and tap Remove App > Delete App

I don't see an install option. Confirm you are accessing Monize over HTTPS, that you are using a supported browser, and that the site is fully loaded. Some browsers require a short interaction with the page before offering installation. The app shows stale content after an update. Close and reopen the installed window to let the service worker pick up the new version. On desktop you can also right-click the app icon and reload. I want to reinstall after uninstalling. Clear the site's cache and service worker data in your browser, then revisit Monize to see the install prompt again.

Once you have Monize installed and your first account created, here are recommended next steps: Migrating from Microsoft Money? Follow the detailed Importing from Microsoft Money guide -- Monize reads your .mny file directly Migrating from Quicken? Follow the detailed Importing from Quicken guide Set up your categories -- Customize the default categories in Categories and Payees Add your accounts -- Create all your financial accounts in Accounts Schedule recurring transactions -- Set up your bills and regular deposits in Bills and Deposits Explore reports -- Check out the Reports section to see what insights are available Import from your bank -- Bring in CSV, OFX/QFX or QIF downloads with Importing Transactions Secure your account -- Set up two-factor authentication and review the other options in Settings and Security

This guide covers importing transactions from bank-exported CSV files, OFX/QFX files, and Quicken QIF files. For complete migration guides, see Importing from Quicken and Importing from Microsoft Money .

Monize can import transactions from files downloaded from your bank or financial institution, or exported from other personal finance software. This is useful for: Regularly importing new transactions from your bank Importing historical transactions from a bank statement download Consolidating accounts from multiple institutions Moving your history across from Quicken or Microsoft Money The import process uses a step-by-step wizard that guides you through file upload, column mapping (for CSV), account selection, category, security and transfer-account mapping, and a review before anything is written. A row of numbered circles at the top shows where you are; only the steps your file needs are shown. Tip Want your bank's transactions to arrive on their own? Settings > Bank Sync connects a bank account through Open Banking and imports its booked transactions daily or on demand, with the same payee matching and rules described here.

Format Extension Description CSV .csv Comma-separated values. Flexible format -- requires column mapping. Banking or investment (brokerage) transactions. OFX .ofx Open Financial Exchange. Standardized format used by most banks. QFX .qfx Quicken Financial Exchange. Identical to OFX with a Quicken-specific wrapper. QIF .qif Quicken Interchange Format. Supports both Microsoft Money and Quicken exports. See Importing Quicken QIF Files and Importing from Microsoft Money . QMTF .qmtf Quicken for Mac's transfer file. It is QIF under another extension and imports the same way. Microsoft Money .mny A whole Microsoft Money file, imported directly. It has its own wizard -- see Importing from Microsoft Money . You can select several files of the same type at once for a bulk import. Files of different types cannot be mixed in one import, and a .mny file is always imported on its own.

Navigate to Tools > Import Transactions to open the import wizard. A Before you import notice at the top links to the Quicken and Microsoft Money guides. Click the upload area to pick your files, or drag them from your computer and drop them onto it. A file the wizard cannot read is refused with its name, before anything is uploaded. You can also start an import from a specific account: on the Accounts page, open the account for editing and click Import at the bottom of the form. The import page then shows "Importing to: account name " and uses that account as the destination. For a single QIF, OFX or CSV file the account selection step is skipped entirely.

When Monize is installed as an app (see Installing as a Progressive Web App ), you can share a bank download to it from your phone's or computer's share sheet. Choose Import as a statement on the Shared with Monize screen and the wizard opens with the files already loaded, exactly as if you had picked them here. Nothing is imported until you click the import button on the review step.
CSV is the most flexible import format. Because CSV files have no standard column layout, you must tell Monize which columns contain the date, amount, payee, and other fields.

Click the upload area or drag your CSV file(s) onto it Monize reads the file and extracts the column headers and sample rows You can select multiple CSV files for bulk import; they are all read with the mapping you set up for the first one File Format: Monize auto-detects the delimiter (comma, semicolon, or tab) and the date format. You can override both in the next step.

This step is unique to CSV imports. You configure how Monize interprets your CSV columns. At the top of the mapping step, an options bar lets you configure: Option Description First row is header Checkbox. When checked, the first row is treated as column headers and excluded from import. Delimiter Dropdown: Comma (,), Semicolon (;), or Tab. Changing the delimiter re-parses the file. Date Format Dropdown with common formats plus a Custom... option. Auto-detected from sample data. Format Example Notes MM/DD/YYYY 03/15/2026 US format (default if ambiguous) DD/MM/YYYY 15/03/2026 International format YYYY-MM-DD 2026-03-15 ISO format YYYY-DD-MM 2026-15-03 Alternate ISO Custom... DD.MM.YYYY Enter any pattern using YYYY/YY, MM, DD tokens with any separator (-, /, .) Monize auto-detects the date format from sample data. If dates appear wrong, select the correct format from the dropdown or enter a custom pattern. A table shows the first 5 rows of your CSV file with column headers. Use this to verify the delimiter and header settings are correct, and to identify which columns contain which data. Monize automatically suggests column mappings based on your CSV headers. It recognizes common header names such as "Date", "Transaction Date" or "Posting Date"; "Amount"; "Debit"/"Withdrawal" and "Credit"/"Deposit"; "Payee", "Description" or "Merchant"; "Category" and "Subcategory"; "Memo" or "Notes"; "Reference", "Check Number" or "Transaction ID"; "Tags" or "Labels"; and "Status" or "Cleared". You can review and adjust the suggested mappings before proceeding. Map your CSV columns to transaction fields using dropdowns. Each dropdown lists the columns found in your file, or Not mapped . Field Required Description File contains -- Banking transactions or Investment transactions (see Importing Investment CSV Files ) Date Yes The transaction date column Amount type Yes Single amount column or Separate debit/credit Amount Yes (if single) A single column containing the transaction amount Sign -- How the amount's sign is read (see below) Debit Yes (if separate) The withdrawal/debit column Credit Yes (if separate) The deposit/credit column Payee No The payee or description column Category No A category column (if your bank provides one) Subcategory No A subcategory column for two-level category hierarchy Memo No Additional notes or description Reference Number No Cheque number or reference ID Tags No One or more tags per row. Several tags in one cell are split on the separator the file uses (` , ; or ,`); dashes and slashes stay part of the tag name Reconciliation Status No Values like "cleared", "reconciled", "posted", "void", * or X are mapped automatically. Unknown values import as unreconciled Select the amount type based on how your CSV represents transaction amounts: Single amount column -- One column with positive values for deposits and negative values for withdrawals (or vice versa). This is the most common format. The Sign option offers: As-is (positive = deposit) -- the default Reverse (positive = withdrawal) -- use this for credit card statements where charges appear as positive numbers Use transaction type column -- see below Separate debit/credit -- Two columns: one for withdrawals (debit) and one for deposits (credit). Common in some bank exports. Use transaction type column -- Use a dedicated column in the CSV to determine transaction direction instead of relying on amount sign. When selected: Choose which column contains the type indicator; the values found in it are listed underneath Enter comma-separated keywords for each type: Income keywords: e.g., "Income", "Deposit" (treated as positive amounts) Expense keywords: e.g., "Expense", "Debit" (treated as negative amounts) Transfer-out keywords: e.g., "Transfer-Out" (money leaving account) Transfer-in keywords: e.g., "Transfer-In" (money entering account) Optionally choose a Transfer account column naming the account each transfer goes to or comes from. It defaults to the Category column. Keyword matching is case-insensitive Amount Parsing: Monize handles currency symbols ($, £, €, ¥, ₹), thousands separators, European decimal commas ( 18,36 is 18.36 and 1.234,56 is 1234.56), and parenthesized negatives -- e.g., ($50.00) is treated as -$50.00 . A single separator followed by exactly three digits, such as 1,234 , is read as a thousands separator. See Transfer Detection below for details on configuring rules that automatically identify transfer transactions in your CSV data. See Saved Column Mappings below for details on saving and reusing your column mapping configuration.

Choose which Monize account the transactions should be imported into. Select from the Import into account dropdown. Monize pre-selects the account whose name best matches the file name, or else an account of the type the file suggests Or click + Create new account to create a new account inline: enter the Account name , Account type and Currency , then click Create . The new account is selected as the destination straight away Auto-Matching: If you navigated to the import page from a specific account, that account is pre-selected and, for a single file, this step is skipped. When you import several files at once, the step lists every file with its transaction count and a destination dropdown (with + Create new under it). Files matched to an account by name are shown in green; files Monize could only guess for are shown in amber, so you know which ones to check.

If your CSV file has a category column, Monize extracts the unique category values and asks you to map them to existing Monize categories or create new ones. A summary line counts the categories that need attention, those matched to categories, and those matched to loans. Categories are then displayed in groups: Needs attention (amber border) -- Categories that could not be auto-matched Auto-matched to loan accounts (shown expanded) -- Categories whose name matches a loan or mortgage account; their transactions are imported as payments to that account Auto-matched to categories (collapsed) -- Categories that matched existing Monize categories. Click Show n auto-matched to categories to check or change them For each category, you can: Map to existing -- Select an existing Monize category Or create new -- Enter a new category name. A Parent category dropdown then appears: leave it at No parent (top-level) , pick an existing category, or choose + Create new parent... and name it Skip -- Leave the dropdown at Skip (no category) ; transactions import without a category This is a loan payment -- Tick it to send the category's transactions to a loan as payments. Pick the loan under Select existing loan , or create one with Or create new loan , its Loan type (Loan or Mortgage), Institution and Initial loan amount (the original principal) No Category Column? If you did not map a category column, this step is skipped. Payee default categories are still applied automatically during import (see Payee Matching During Import ).

If transfer detection rules matched any transactions (see Transfer Detection ), you map the account names they produced to Monize accounts. Each name already matching an account is filled in (green); for any other, pick one under Map to existing , or type a name under Or create new and choose its Account type and Currency .

The review step shows a summary of the import: File name, transaction count and target account (for a bulk import, each file with its count and target, and the total) Categories: total, mapped, new to create, and those mapped to loan accounts or new loans Transfer accounts and securities: total, mapped, and new to create Click Import Transactions to execute the import. Each file is imported inside a database transaction -- if the import fails, none of its changes are kept. A single row that cannot be imported is counted as an error and the rest of the file still imports.

After a successful import, you see: Metric Description Imported Transactions successfully imported Skipped Rows not imported because they are already there: an OFX row imported before ("already imported"), or the other side of a transfer that is already recorded ("transfer already recorded"). The skipped rows are listed with their date, amount and payee Errors Transactions that failed (with error details) Categories created New categories added Accounts created New accounts added Payees created New payees added Securities created New securities added For a bulk import, an Overall Summary is followed by Per-File Results : each file in green, or in red with its first three error messages. If the import created a loan or mortgage account without scheduled payments, a Set Up Recurring Payments box lists it with a Set Up Payments button, so the loan's progress can be tracked from then on. Click View Transactions (or View Investments after an investment import) to see the accounts you just imported into, or Import More Files to start again.

A brokerage's activity export can be imported as investment transactions. When the file's headers include an action, a security and a quantity column, the mapping step switches File contains to Investment transactions by itself; you can change it either way. In investment mode the column mapping asks for: Field Required Description Action Yes What each row is: buy, sell, dividend and so on Security (Symbol or Name) Yes The ticker or the security's name Quantity No Number of shares Price No Price per share Commission No Commission and fees Amount No The total of the row Rows are classified by an exact (case-insensitive) match of the action column against keyword lists for Buy , Sell , Dividend , Interest , Capital gain , Reinvest , Stock split , Shares transferred in , Shares transferred out , Add shares , Remove shares , Cash deposit and Cash withdrawal . The step lists the action values found in the file and any it does not recognize; click Customize action keywords to add your broker's wording to a list. A value that matches nothing is imported as a cash deposit or withdrawal on the account's linked cash account, by the sign of its amount. Choose the investment account as the destination; the wizard then continues with Map Securities . The review step adds an Investment Transactions box counting each action and warning about rows that will import as cash, purchases without a price, and rows that cannot be imported at all (for example a sell with no price or proceeds), so you can go back and adjust the mapping. Transfer detection rules do not apply in investment mode.

OFX (Open Financial Exchange) and QFX (Quicken Financial Exchange) are standardized file formats that banks use to provide transaction downloads. Unlike CSV, these formats have a defined structure -- no column mapping is needed. Most banks offer OFX or QFX downloads from their online banking portals, typically under a "Download transactions" or "Export" option.

h: How OFX/QFX Import Differs from CSV
x: Aspect CSV OFX/QFX Column mapping Required Not needed (fixed format) Date format User-selected or auto-detected Automatic (embedded in file) Payee From mapped column From NAME field in file Memo From mapped column From MEMO field (if different from NAME) Category From mapped column (optional) Not provided -- mapped during import or via payee defaults Cleared status From mapped column (optional) All transactions marked as cleared (posted) Transfer detection Via user-defined rules Automatic for XFER transaction types Amount handling User configures sign and column Automatic (signed amounts in file) Reference number From mapped column (optional) From CHECKNUM field Re-importing the same rows Imported again Skipped (see below)

The OFX/QFX import follows the same wizard but skips the column mapping step: Upload -- Select your .ofx or .qfx file(s) Select Account -- Choose the destination account Map Categories -- Map any categories found (OFX files rarely include categories) Map Transfer Accounts -- Map accounts for transfer transactions Review and Import -- Confirm and execute Complete -- View results

Every OFX row carries the bank's own transaction ID. Monize remembers it, so when you import a download that overlaps one you imported before, the rows already in the account are skipped and listed under Skipped rows as "already imported". You can therefore download a generous date range each time without creating duplicates. A row you have since edited to a different date or amount is no longer recognized and imports again. Statement Type Description BANKMSGSRSV1 Chequing and savings accounts CREDITCARDMSGSRSV1 Credit card accounts Note: Investment statements (INVSTMTMSGSRSV1) are not supported in OFX format. Use QIF or a brokerage CSV export for investment account imports. Monize recognizes the following OFX transaction types: OFX Type Handling DEBIT Standard withdrawal CREDIT Standard deposit CHECK Cheque transaction DEP Deposit ATM ATM withdrawal/deposit POS Point-of-sale transaction XFER Transfer (see OFX Transfer Detection ) INT Interest DIV Dividend FEE Fee SRVCHG Service charge PAYMENT Payment OTHER Other transaction

Monize supports QIF files exported from Quicken, including both individual account exports and Quicken's full-file export (which contains all accounts, categories, and tags in a single QIF file), as well as Quicken for Mac's .qmtf files. Both layouts are auto-detected. Important Future-Dated Transactions Monize does not currently support importing future-dated transactions. If your Quicken QIF file contains scheduled or future transactions, you must remove them from the QIF file before importing. See the full guide for details. Key Quicken QIF features supported: Colon-separated category hierarchy (e.g., Food:Groceries ) -- parent/child categories created automatically Full-file export -- all accounts, category definitions ( !Type:Cat ), and tag definitions ( !Type:Tag ) in a single file Single-account export -- one file per account, with bulk import support Date padding -- Quicken's space-padded dates (e.g., 2/ 4/19 ) handled automatically Tags -- extracted from the / separator in category fields Cleared status -- Quicken's * / c (cleared) and X / R (reconciled) flags For the complete step-by-step guide including exporting from Quicken, import order, and troubleshooting, see Importing from Quicken .

Feature CSV OFX/QFX Ease of setup Requires column mapping No mapping needed Flexibility Works with any CSV layout Fixed format Date format Must be specified Automatic Amount sign Configurable (normal, reverse, or type column) Automatic Categories Can map from file column Not in file -- use payee defaults or rules Transfer detection Rule-based (user configures) Automatic for XFER type Investment transactions Yes, with an action column No Saved presets Yes (saved column mappings) Not needed Cleared status Optional status column Always cleared Overlapping downloads Imported again Rows already imported are skipped Best for Banks with non-standard exports, brokerages, custom data Standard bank downloads

Since CSV files have no standard way to indicate transfers, Monize lets you define rules that identify transfer transactions based on patterns in the payee or category fields. Click Add Rule under Transfer Detection Rules on the column mapping step to add one. Each rule reads " Field contains Pattern as transfer from/to Account ": Part Description Field Which column to match: Payee or Category Pattern Text to search for (case-insensitive, "contains" matching) Account The Monize account the transfer goes to or comes from Click Remove to delete a rule. Field Pattern Target Account Matches Payee Transfer to Savings Savings "Transfer to Savings - Jan" Payee INTERAC e-Transfer Chequing "INTERAC e-Transfer JOHN DOE" Category Transfer Savings Any transaction where category contains "Transfer" When a rule matches, the transaction is: Marked as a transfer Linked to the target account Category is cleared (transfers do not have categories) Rules are evaluated in order. The first matching rule wins. Tip: Transfer rules are saved along with your column mapping preset, so you only need to configure them once per bank format.

OFX files include a transaction type field. Transactions with type XFER are automatically treated as transfers. The payee name (NAME field) is used as the transfer account name, which you map during the import wizard.

If you regularly import CSV files from the same bank, you can save your column mapping configuration as a named preset to avoid re-mapping each time. Configure your column mapping, date format, delimiter, and transfer rules Click Save Current in the Saved Mappings section Enter a descriptive name (e.g., "TD Chequing CSV", "Visa Statement") Click Save (or press Enter) If a mapping with the same name already exists, it is overwritten (a "Will overwrite" warning appears). Select a saved mapping from the Load a saved mapping... dropdown All settings are restored: column assignments, delimiter, date format, header toggle, and transfer rules Click the x button next to any saved mapping name to delete it. Saved mappings include transfer rules. When you save a column mapping preset, the transfer detection rules are saved with it.

During import, Monize automatically resolves payee names using the following process: Exact match -- If a payee with the same name already exists, the transaction is assigned to it Alias match -- If a payee alias pattern matches the imported name (see Payee Aliases ), the transaction is assigned to the canonical payee Create new -- If no match is found, a new payee is created When a payee is matched (by name or alias), its default category is applied to the transaction -- unless the transaction already has a category from the import file. Payee name cleanup: In a CSV import, all-caps payee names are converted to Proper Case (e.g., "STARBUCKS" becomes "Starbucks"). OFX and QIF payees are kept as the file spells them. This matching process is identical for CSV, OFX/QFX, and QIF imports. To make the most of it, set up payee aliases before your first import (see Payee Aliases ).

After a transaction is imported, your rules set to run on import ( Tools > Rules ) are applied to it: they can set its category, payee or description, add or remove tags, or send it to the AI review queue. A rule never changes an amount. The rule sees the payee text as it was in the file, before alias matching. Transfers created by the import are not passed through rules. See Rules for writing and testing them.

Create your accounts in Monize first, so they are available as import destinations (or create them inline during the import) Set up payee aliases for common payees that appear with varying names in bank files (e.g., "STARBUCKS #1234" vs "STARBUCKS #5678") Set default categories on payees, or write rules, to automate categorization during import

Save a column mapping the first time you import from a bank -- it saves time on future imports Set up transfer rules if your bank includes inter-account transfers in the CSV Use the "Reverse (positive = withdrawal)" sign for credit card statements where charges are positive numbers Prefer OFX/QFX if your bank offers it -- overlapping downloads are then de-duplicated for you

Import all files for the same period at once for better transfer matching After import, review uncategorized transactions ( Reports > Uncategorized Transactions ) Use the Recalculate button on the Net Worth report after large imports to update balance snapshots

Cause: The date format was auto-detected incorrectly. Solution: For CSV, change the Date Format in the options bar, or enter a custom pattern. Monize defaults to MM/DD/YYYY when dates are ambiguous (e.g., both parts are 12 or less). OFX dates are unambiguous. For a QIF full-file export, change the Date Format on the review step; a single-account QIF file's date format is detected from the file itself.
Cause: Your bank exports withdrawals as positive numbers (common for credit card statements). Solution: In the CSV column mapping step, change the Sign option to "Reverse (positive = withdrawal)".
Cause: The delimiter was auto-detected incorrectly (e.g., a semicolon-delimited file detected as comma). Solution: Change the delimiter in the options bar and the file will be re-parsed.

Cause: Importing the same file twice, or overlapping date ranges between imports. Solution: OFX/QFX imports skip rows they already imported. CSV and QIF imports do not detect duplicates (apart from the second side of a transfer that is already recorded), so import each period once. Use the Duplicate Transaction Finder report to identify and remove duplicates.

Cause (CSV): No transfer rule matched the transaction, or the rule pattern did not match. Solution: Check your transfer rules. Matching is case-insensitive "contains" -- the pattern must appear somewhere in the payee or category text. Cause (OFX): The transaction type was not XFER. Solution: Manually edit the transaction and convert it to a transfer.
Cause: The file may use an unsupported OFX statement type (e.g., investment statements). Solution: Try exporting as CSV from your bank instead, or use QIF format for investment accounts.

h: "All files must be the same type"
x: Cause: A bulk import mixed QIF, OFX and CSV files. Solution: Import each type separately.

Cause: Very large files (near the 10 MB limit) or files with thousands of transactions. Solution: The import has a 5-minute timeout. If the file is too large, try splitting it into smaller date ranges.

This is the complete guide to migrating your financial data from Quicken to Monize using QIF file exports. It covers exporting from Quicken, preparing your data, and importing into Monize. For importing from other sources using CSV or OFX/QFX files, see Importing Transactions . For migrating from Microsoft Money, see Importing from Microsoft Money .

Quicken uses QIF (Quicken Interchange Format) for data export. Monize includes a comprehensive QIF import wizard that handles: Regular banking transactions (chequing, savings, credit cards) Investment transactions (buy, sell, dividends, splits, reinvestments) Split transactions (multiple categories per transaction) Account-to-account transfers Category creation and mapping (with colon-separated hierarchy support) Tag definitions from Quicken's tag system Security creation and mapping Multi-account full-file exports (all accounts in a single QIF file) Monize auto-detects whether a QIF file is a single-account export or a full-file export and adapts the import wizard accordingly. Quicken for Mac's .qmtf transfer files are QIF under another extension, with section headers in capitals and Mac line endings; Monize reads them exactly like a .qif file.

Warning Future-Dated Transactions Are Not Supported Monize does not support importing future-dated transactions. Quicken's QIF export defaults to a far-future end date that includes scheduled and future transactions. When exporting, always set the "to" date to today's date to exclude them. See Removing Future-Dated Transactions if you need to clean up a file that was already exported with future transactions.
Quicken offers two ways to export your data as QIF files.

Export one account at a time: In Quicken, select the account you want to export Go to File > Export > QIF File Important: Change the "to" date to today's date . Quicken defaults this to a far-future date (e.g., 31/12/2099), which will include scheduled and future-dated transactions that Monize cannot import. Select the transactions to include Save the .qif file with a descriptive name (e.g., Chequing.qif , Visa.qif ) Repeat for each account Investment Accounts: Unlike Microsoft Money, Quicken's QIF export for investment accounts includes both securities transactions and cash transactions in a single file. You do not need to export twice.

Export your entire Quicken data file at once: In Quicken, go to File > Export > QIF File Select All Accounts (or select multiple accounts) Important: Change the "to" date to today's date . Quicken defaults this to a far-future date (e.g., 31/12/2099), which will include scheduled and future-dated transactions that Monize cannot import. Set it to today's date to export only past and present transactions. Ensure categories and tags are included in the export Save the .qif file A full-file export produces a single QIF file that contains: Category definitions ( !Type:Cat sections) -- your full category hierarchy with tax-related flags Tag definitions ( !Type:Tag sections) -- your Quicken tags Account blocks ( !Account sections) -- each account's transactions grouped together Transaction data -- all transactions across all included accounts

Method Best For Advantages Disadvantages Single-account Selective migration, importing specific accounts Full control over what to import; can import in a specific order Must handle transfer linking across separate imports Full-file Complete migration from Quicken One file, one import; transfers auto-linked; categories and tags included All-or-nothing

The easiest fix is to re-export from Quicken with the "to" date set to today. See Full-File Export for details. If you prefer to fix an already-exported file, open it in a text editor (Notepad, VS Code, etc.) and delete any transactions with future dates. Each transaction looks like this: D3/14/2026 T-45.00 PGrocery Store LFood:Groceries ^ The D line is the date and ^ marks the end of the transaction. Delete the entire block (from D through ^ ) for any transaction dated after today, then save the file.
Navigate to Tools > Import Transactions to begin.

If you are importing multiple single-account QIF files, the order matters for transfer linking. Import in this order: 1. Asset Accounts | 2. Bank, Credit Card and Line of Credit Accounts (Home Currency) | 3. Bank, Credit Card and Line of Credit Accounts (Foreign Currency) | 4. Investment Accounts Monize matches pending transfers from previously imported files, so importing accounts with the most outgoing transfers first ensures correct linking. Tip: Select all your QIF files at once for bulk import. Monize processes them sequentially and coordinates transfer matching across files.

Click the upload area or drag your QIF files onto it You can select multiple files at once for bulk import Monize parses each file and extracts: Account type detected from the QIF header Number of transactions Date range of transactions Categories found (including colon-separated hierarchy) Transfer accounts referenced Securities found (for investment files)

For each QIF file, specify which Monize account the transactions should be imported into. A gray information box shows: File: The filename being imported Transactions: Number of transactions found Date Range: Earliest to latest transaction dates Detected Type: Account type from the QIF header (e.g., Chequing, Investment, Credit Card) Choose from the Import into account dropdown: For investment QIF files (detected type: Investment), only brokerage accounts are shown, and a blue note says so For regular QIF files , all non-brokerage accounts are shown Auto-Matching: Monize matches QIF file names to account names automatically, so Visa.qif lands on your "Visa" account. When several files are uploaded together, each gets its own dropdown; files matched by name are shown in green and guesses in amber. If the destination account does not exist: Click + Create new account ( + Create new for a file in a bulk import) Fill in the Account name (pre-filled from the file name), Account type and Currency Click Create The new account is auto-selected as the destination. Creating an Investment account creates its linked cash and brokerage pair; an investment file goes into the brokerage side. Monize detects the date format from the dates in the file, including Quicken's space-padded dates. There is no override for a single-account file, so if the dates come out swapped (day and month), re-export from Quicken with your system's date format set to the format you expect. A full-file export has a Date Format dropdown on its review step (see Part 4 ). Quicken Date Quirk: Quicken may pad single-digit days with spaces (e.g., 2/ 4/19 instead of 2/4/19 ). Monize handles this automatically.

Quicken uses colon-separated category paths (e.g., Food:Groceries , Auto:Fuel , Fees & Charges:Bank Fee ). Monize automatically parses this hierarchy and matches each path against your existing categories. A summary line counts the categories that need attention and those matched, and they are displayed in three groups: Needs attention (amber border) -- Categories that could not be auto-matched. Require your input. Auto-matched to loan accounts (shown expanded) -- Matched to loan or mortgage account names (imported as payments to the loan account). Auto-matched to categories (collapsed) -- Successfully matched to existing Monize categories. Click Show n auto-matched to categories to review or change them. For a colon path Monize cannot match, the row comes already filled in to create the last level under its parent: Auto:Parking suggests a new "Parking" under an existing "Auto", or under a new parent "Auto" if you have none. Accept the suggestion, or change it. For each unmatched category, you can: Map to existing -- Select an existing Monize category Or create new -- Enter a new category name, then pick a Parent category (or + Create new parent... ) Skip -- Leave the dropdown at Skip (no category) ; categorize later This is a loan payment -- Tick it to import the category's transactions as payments to an existing loan, or to a new loan you name with its type, institution and initial amount When Monize creates new categories from Quicken's colon-separated paths: It detects the parent-child relationship from the colon separator Creates the parent category if it does not exist Creates the child category under the correct parent Deduplicates parents across multiple children For example, importing categories Food:Groceries , Food:Restaurants , and Food:Coffee creates one "Food" parent with three children.

This step appears only for investment QIF files containing security references. When you reach the step, Monize looks up every security it could not match to one of yours (the line "Looking up securities..." shows while it runs) and fills in what it finds. A row shows a green border once it is ready and an amber one while it needs attention. For each security, you can: Map to existing -- Select from the dropdown of existing Monize securities (it starts at Skip (no security) ) Or create new (symbol) -- Enter the symbol, the Security name , the Security type (Stock, ETF, Mutual Fund, Bond, Option, GIC, Cryptocurrency, Cash/Money Market or Other), the Exchange and the Currency . Picking an exchange sets the currency that exchange trades in Lookup -- Search again by name or symbol. When several securities fit, you choose the right one from a list Your preferred exchanges ( Settings > Preferences ) are tried first.

This step appears when the QIF file references transfers to other accounts (using Quicken's [Account Name] notation). It is skipped for investment files, whose transfers go through the linked cash account. For each referenced account (names that match one of your accounts are filled in already): Map to existing -- Select from the dropdown of existing Monize accounts Or create new -- Enter the account name, then choose its Account type and Currency Bulk Import Tip: If you are importing all files at once, transfers between accounts in the batch are linked automatically. You only need to map accounts that are not part of the current import.

The review step shows a summary of everything that will happen: Files and transaction counts Target accounts Categories, transfer accounts and securities: how many are mapped and how many will be created Click Import Transactions to execute. Each file is imported inside a database transaction -- if the import fails, none of its changes are kept. A single transaction that cannot be imported is counted as an error and the rest of the file still imports.

After import, Monize displays: Metric Description Imported Transactions successfully imported Skipped Transfers already recorded from the other account, listed row by row Errors Transactions that failed (with details) Categories created New categories added Accounts created New accounts added Payees created New payees added Securities created New securities added If a loan or mortgage account was created without scheduled payments, Set Up Payments lets you add them straight away. View Transactions (or View Investments ) opens the accounts you just imported into; Import More Files starts again.

h: Part 4: Importing a Full-File QIF Export
x: When you upload a full-file QIF export, Monize detects it automatically (by the presence of several !Account sections or a !Type:Cat category list) and adapts the import wizard.

Aspect Single-Account Import Full-File Import Account selection Choose one account per file None: each account in the file is matched to your account of the same name, or created Category mapping Map each category None: the !Type:Cat definitions (and any other categories the transactions use) are matched to your categories of the same name, or created with their hierarchy Tag definitions Extracted from transaction data Created from !Type:Tag sections and the transactions Transfer linking Across files in a bulk import Automatic within the single file Date format Detected Detected, with a dropdown to change it Number of files One or more One file

Upload -- Select your full-file .qif export (one file on its own; several files are treated as single-account exports) Review -- The Multi-Account QIF Import step summarizes the file ("This file contains 3 accounts, 6 categories, 2 tags, and 6 transactions") and lists: Currency for New Accounts -- the currency every account the import creates is given Date Format -- detected from the file; the sample dates underneath show how it was read Accounts -- each account with its type, transaction count and date range Categories -- grouped into Expense and Income Tags -- the tags that will be created Choose missing account types -- if the file does not say what type an account is, a Choose a type dropdown appears beside it, and the import cannot start until each one has a type Map Securities -- if the file holds investment accounts, the notice says how many securities need mapping; click Next: Map Securities and map them as in Step 4 , then click Import All there Import -- otherwise click Import All on the review step Complete -- View results An account in the file that has the same name as one of your accounts is imported into it rather than created again (for an investment account, the " name - Cash" account counts too). Every other account is created, an investment account as its linked cash and brokerage pair. Tip: Full-file import is the easiest way to migrate from Quicken. All transfers between accounts are automatically linked, and your complete category and tag hierarchy is preserved.
After importing your Quicken data, take these steps to verify and finalize your migration.

Compare each account's current balance in Monize against Quicken. If balances do not match: Check the opening balance -- it should match the balance as of the first transaction date Look for missing or duplicate transactions Check that transfers between accounts were matched correctly

Navigate to Investments Check that each holding shows the correct quantity and cost basis Compare against your Quicken portfolio summary If any securities were auto-created, update their symbols and exchange information

Securities created during import use the symbol, exchange and type entered on the Map Securities step, and get price updates like any other security. If one was created with a guessed symbol: Navigate to Tools > Securities Edit the security to correct its symbol, exchange, and type Prices are fetched for the corrected symbol from then on

Navigate to Tools > Categories and review the category hierarchy. Categories imported from Quicken preserve the colon-separated hierarchy (e.g., Food:Groceries becomes "Groceries" under parent "Food"). Verify the hierarchy looks correct and reorganize if needed.

Quicken's QIF export does not include scheduled or recurring transactions. You must recreate these manually: Navigate to Bills & Deposits Create each recurring bill and deposit See Bills and Deposits for details
Run the Uncategorized Transactions report ( Reports > Uncategorized Transactions ) to find any transactions imported without a category.
Navigate to the Dashboard and check the Net Worth chart. Click Recalculate on the Net Worth report if needed to refresh balance snapshots after import.

If your import did not go as expected and you want to start fresh, you can delete all your financial data without losing your user account or settings. Navigate to Settings Scroll to the Danger Zone section Click "Delete Data..." Check all four optional boxes (Accounts, Categories, Payees, Currency preferences) for a completely clean slate Enter your password to confirm This removes all transactions, accounts, categories, securities, budgets, and other financial data. Your user account, preferences, and security settings (2FA, trusted devices) are preserved. You can then re-import your QIF files. For more details, see Settings and Security > Danger Zone .
Understanding the QIF format can help when troubleshooting or manually editing files.

Cause: The QIF file contains transactions with dates in the future. Solution: Remove future-dated transactions from the QIF file before importing. See Removing Future-Dated Transactions . Alternatively, re-export from Quicken with a date range ending on or before today.

Cause: The date format was detected incorrectly (e.g., MM/DD was interpreted as DD/MM). Solution: For a full-file export, change the Date Format dropdown on the review step. A single-account file's format is detected from its dates; if they are all ambiguous (every day 12 or less), re-export from Quicken with an unambiguous date range or format. Quicken typically uses MM/DD/YYYY format.

Cause: The colon separator in category names was not detected. Solution: Verify the QIF file uses standard colon-separated categories (e.g., LFood:Groceries ). If categories use a different separator, they will be imported as flat names. You can reorganize them manually in Tools > Categories .

Cause: Importing the same file twice, or transfer transactions appearing in both accounts. Solution: Monize skips the second side of a transfer that is already recorded when importing the other account If duplicates still appear, use the Duplicate Transaction Finder report For future imports, import all related files in a single bulk operation

Cause: Transfer accounts were not mapped correctly, or files were imported in separate sessions. Solution: Import all files at once using bulk import For full-file exports, transfers are linked automatically Manually link unmatched transfers by editing the transactions

h: Investment Securities Not Found During Lookup
x: Cause: The security name in Quicken does not match market data. Solution: During the Map Securities step, click Lookup after typing the symbol instead of the name If lookup fails, manually enter the symbol, name, type, and exchange After import, verify securities in Tools > Securities

Cause: The opening balance transaction in the QIF does not match expected starting point. Solution: Navigate to Accounts Edit the account Adjust the opening balance and opening date The current balance will be recalculated

Cause: Very large QIF file (near the 10 MB limit or thousands of transactions). Solution: The import has a 5-minute timeout. If the file is too large, re-export from Quicken with a smaller date range.

The QIF format and Quicken export have limitations.
