No password or invite step, and their credentials are never touched. New email, you set the password Optionally enter a First name and Last name , then a Password A new user is created with that password. Share it with the delegate out-of-band; they can change it after signing in. New email, send an email invite Optionally enter the names, then turn on Send an email invite instead of setting a password A new user is created with no password. An invite email is sent containing a one-time link valid for 24 hours; the delegate sets their own password. Note The password must meet Monize's standard requirements: at least 12 characters, with an uppercase letter, a lowercase letter, a number and a special character. Passwords are also checked against the Have I Been Pwned breach database. The email invite needs outbound email; on a server without it, set a password instead. If the address check itself fails (for example, the server could not be reached), the dialog says so and pauses adding the delegate until a Check again succeeds. That way an existing person's password can never be overwritten by mistake. Important Joint access and account type. A delegate you create here with a password or invite is an owner-managed identity. Joint sharing is offered only for delegates who are full Monize accounts of their own, so if you intend to share an account jointly with your spouse, have them register (or add them by their existing email) rather than creating a credential for them. After the delegate is added, they appear in the list with zero accounts granted. The next step is to configure permissions.

h: Turning a Delegate Login Into a Full Account
x: A delegate you created with a password can later make the login their own: they open the registration page, enter the same email, and register with the password you gave them (or with a new password, entering yours to prove they hold the login). From then on the login is theirs -- you can no longer reset its password, and once they have data of their own you can share accounts with them jointly. A login protected by two-factor authentication cannot be claimed this way; that person simply signs in.

From the delegate's row in the Shared Access list, click Edit access to open the permissions dialog. It has three tabs: Accounts , Sections and Shared data . Nothing changes until you click Save ; closing the dialog with unsaved changes asks before discarding them.

Choose which accounts the delegate can see, and what they can do with each. Each account row has five toggles: Toggle Meaning Read See the account, its balance, and its transactions Create Add new transactions to the account Edit Modify existing transactions in the account Delete Delete transactions from the account Joint The account appears natively in the delegate's own account list, register and net worth -- no context switching. See Joint Accounts . Read is required for Create, Edit, Delete, and Joint. On an account row those four toggles stay greyed out until Read is on, and turning Read off clears them. If you grant no Read access at all, the delegate sees nothing for that account. Accounts are grouped by type (Chequing, Savings, Credit Card, etc.), and each group has a Grant all row whose toggles switch a column on or off for every account in the group -- turning on Create, Edit, Delete or Joint there turns on Read as well. This lets you scope access broadly, for example sharing all chequing accounts with your spouse while keeping investment accounts private. Joint is disabled for delegates who are not full Monize accounts. Hovering the toggle explains why: "Joint accounts can only be shared with users who have their own Monize account" . Note You can only share what you own. Accounts that somebody else shared with you do not appear in this tab at all, so a joint account can never be re-shared onward -- only its owner can share it.

Section toggles give the delegate read-only access to whole feature areas of the application: Section What it controls Bills & Deposits Scheduled transactions for the accounts they can read Investments Holdings and investment transactions for the accounts they can read Budgets Budget figures, read-only Reports Built-in and custom reports, read-only AI Assistant Natural-language questions answered with your configured AI provider Warranties Your warranties, their documents and their claims, the Warranties link in Tools and the dashboard widget. A warranty's linked purchase appears only when its account is one the delegate can read. See Warranties . Sections apply to the delegate while acting as you . They have no bearing on joint accounts, which live in the delegate's own context. A section is only useful if the delegate also has Read access to the accounts that feed it. For example, granting Reports without granting Read on any account produces empty reports. Note AI Assistant. The assistant reads across every account and section, so it only answers for a delegate who can read all of your accounts and has every other section turned on. With anything less, the section is granted but the assistant does not answer. When it does answer, the delegate uses your configured AI provider and counts against your AI usage.

Categories, payees, and tags are shared reference data across all of your accounts. This tab controls whether the delegate can change them: Resource Toggles Payees Create, Edit, Delete Categories Create, Edit, Delete Tags Create, Edit, Delete Read access to all three is always allowed -- delegates need to see payees, categories, and tags to make sense of any transaction. A delegate sees Payees , Categories or Tags in the Tools menu only when they hold at least one of these permissions for it. Tip A common setup is to enable Create for all three but leave Edit and Delete off. This lets the delegate enter transactions naturally (creating new payees as needed) without being able to rename or remove existing entries that affect your historical data. The Payees > Create and Categories > Create permissions also govern whether a grantee may create a new payee or category while entering a transaction on a joint account.

Added in v1.14.0. Plain delegation means acting as the other person: you switch context, see their ledger, and switch back. That is right for a bookkeeper and wrong for a couple sharing a chequing account. Turning on Joint for an account (on top of Read ) makes that account appear in the other person's own data as though it were theirs. Nothing to remember, nothing to switch.

Once an account is joint, the grantee sees it in their own context: Account list -- listed alongside their own accounts, with a Joint badge and "Shared by [your name]" . A Shared with me filter switch on the accounts page narrows the list to shared accounts only. Register -- the account's transactions, and (where permitted) the ability to add, edit and delete rows in it Net worth -- included by default; see Net Worth Account detail page -- the balance chart, cash flow, top categories, top payees and balance forecast, computed exactly as the owner sees them What the grantee can do is still your existing per-account grants: Read , Create , Edit , Delete . Those grants are enforced by the server, not merely by hiding buttons. The grantee never gets ownership of the account object. Renaming, closing, reconciling, changing settings on and deleting a joint account are the owner's alone -- those actions are not offered on a joint row and are rejected server-side.

h: Which Account Types Can Be Written To
x: Only everyday banking accounts accept grantee writes. The rest are shared read-only no matter which grant flags are turned on: Account type Shareable as joint Grantee writes Chequing, Savings, Cash, Credit Card, Line of Credit Yes Create / Edit / Delete, as granted Investment, Loan, Mortgage, Asset, Other Yes None -- read-only regardless of the grant flags The effective permission the grantee's screen shows is the grant flags combined with this policy, so the interface and the server can never disagree.

h: Categories, Payees, and Tags on Joint Accounts
x: Every transaction in a joint account belongs to the owner's ledger, even the rows the grantee writes: The grantee picks categories and payees from your lists, not theirs. Their own reference data can never land on your rows. Typing a brand-new payee name creates it on your ledger, but only if the delegation has Payees > Create . Otherwise the transaction is refused with a message asking them to pick one of your existing payees. A new category can be created the same way, on your ledger, when the delegation has Categories > Create . Tags are personal on both sides. The grantee cannot set tags on a joint row; your existing tags on those rows display read-only to them, and tag-based breakdowns stay owner-only. Rows the grantee creates keep their creator attribution, but they are your transactions, on your account, in your reports.

The grantee decides whether a joint account counts toward their net worth, with Exclude from my net worth / Include in my net worth in the account row's menu. That preference is theirs alone: it is invisible to you, and it is never confused with your own "exclude from net worth" setting. Case In the grantee's net worth? Joint account, no exclusion set by the grantee Yes (the default) Joint account the grantee excluded No Joint account you excluded from your net worth Yes -- your flag governs your view only Plain (non-joint) granted account No -- never aggregated into the delegate's own numbers Your own net worth is unchanged in every case.

On your side, a shared account is labelled with how many people it is shared with: The account list row shows a Joint badge and "Shared with N people" The edit account form shows "Joint account shared with N people" with a Manage sharing link straight to Shared Access

h: What Joint Accounts Do Not Include Yet
x: These are deliberate scope cuts, not bugs: Reports (built-in and custom) exclude joint rows AI Assistant and the MCP server exclude joint rows -- both AI surfaces change together, and neither reads them yet Investment breakdowns exclude joint investment accounts (the plain net-worth total still includes them) Attachments, scheduled transactions and investment holdings on a joint account are not natively visible to the grantee Grantees cannot add splits, tags or attachments to joint rows (a split row in a shared account can only be managed by the owner) Grantee CSV / QIF export of joint rows is not available yet Anything in this list is still reachable the old way, if you also grant plain delegated access: the grantee switches into your context and sees it there.

You can transfer money between an account you own and an account shared with you , in either direction and from either side. In the transfer form, the account picker lists Your accounts and, under Shared with you , the other person's accounts you are allowed to move money into, each labelled with its owner. Authorization is the ordinary write grant ( Create / Edit / Delete ) on the shared side. Each leg belongs to its own account's owner, so both ledgers stay self-contained -- balances, net worth, reports and exports keep aggregating only your own rows. Moving a transfer leg between owners is rejected; so are cross-owner split transfers and cross-owner scheduled transfers. The AI Assistant and MCP server cannot create or edit cross-owner transfers; they report a clear error rather than half-doing it.

Everything about joint access is computed from the grants that exist right now . Nothing is copied, so nothing needs repairing. Turn off Joint (or Read , or remove the delegate entirely) and on the grantee's next page load: The account disappears from their list, register, detail pages and net worth -- no leftovers, no tombstones Existing transfers between their account and yours are frozen, not severed . Each side keeps its own leg, the counterpart shows as Hidden account instead of leaking the other person's account details, and neither side can change the amount, date or account through it. Descriptive fields on your own leg stay editable, and the form says why the rest is locked. Deleting your own leg of a frozen transfer removes only your leg and detaches the counterpart, which survives as a one-sided transfer. Rows the grantee created in the account stay in your ledger, untouched -- they were always your rows. Turn Joint back on later and all of the above reverses on its own: the account reappears, the masking lifts, and frozen transfers reconnect with no repair step. Note that re-granting plain Read does not silently restore the joint flag -- you turn it on again deliberately. The Hidden account masking applies everywhere a transfer can be read: lists, transaction detail, exports, and what the AI Assistant and MCP server can see.

When the delegate is acting as you, their navigation is filtered to what they can reach: Transactions appears when they can read at least one of your non-investment accounts; Accounts when they can read at least one account Bills & Deposits , Investments , Budgets and Reports appear only if the corresponding section is on, and the AI menu only with the AI Assistant section (the AI review inbox is never shown to a delegate) In Tools , Payees , Categories and Tags appear only with a matching Shared data permission, and Warranties only with the Warranties section Transactions involving an account the delegate cannot read display the inaccessible side as Hidden account in transfers The delegate can mark accounts as favourites independently of your own favourites -- their dashboard ordering does not affect yours If a delegate has no Monize data of their own and only one person shares with them, they go straight into that person's data after signing in.

A delegate who has more than one place to be -- their own data and yours, or the data of several owners -- sees an amber banner under the navigation bar on every page, with a Switch account dropdown that names the data they are looking at. The dropdown lets the delegate switch between: Their own account (if they have one, labelled "(you)") Each owner who has shared access with them Selecting a different context reloads the page so all data refreshes under the new identity. A delegate with no data of their own and a single owner has nothing to switch between, so the banner is not shown. Note Purely joint delegations are not listed. If everything you shared with someone is joint -- every readable account already appears natively, with no sections and no shared-data permissions -- there is nothing extra to see by switching, so you are not offered as a context. A delegation with nothing readable yet stays listed, so the delegate can still get in once you grant something, and the context somebody is currently acting as is never pulled out from under them. Tip The banner is intentionally visible at all times. It guards against the delegate forgetting which dataset they are looking at and entering information into the wrong account.

If a delegate forgets their password, the owner can issue a new temporary password from the Shared Access list -- but only when the delegate is a delegate-only user . Open Settings > Shared Access Click Reset password on the delegate's row Copy the temporary password (the dialog's Copy button) and share it with the delegate out-of-band. It is not shown again. The delegate signs in with the temporary password and is asked to choose a new one A reset also signs the delegate out everywhere, removes their trusted devices and personal access tokens, and clears any lockout from failed sign-in attempts. The Reset password button is greyed out (hover it for the reason) for delegates who: Have registered their own Monize account (they own their credentials -- you cannot overwrite them) Own financial accounts of their own Are also delegates for a different owner Have the admin role Sign in through single sign-on In any of these cases, the delegate must use the standard Forgot Password flow on the login page. Note Because joint sharing requires a full Monize account, a delegate you share jointly with always manages their own password.

Open Settings > Shared Access Click Remove on the delegate's row Confirm with Remove in the dialog Removing a delegate immediately revokes all of their access: All per-account grants are deleted, including joint flags Every joint account disappears from their own account list, register and net worth Cross-owner transfers between you freeze as described in Unsharing and Re-sharing Their per-account net-worth exclusions for your accounts are discarded along with the grants The delegate's favourite-account list (for your accounts) is removed If the delegate is currently signed in and viewing your data, their next request fails with "Delegated access is no longer valid" and they are signed out If the delegate is a delegate-only user who has never created their own accounts and has no other delegations, their login is also deleted. Otherwise the user remains (they keep their own login and any other delegations) -- only the relationship to your accounts is removed. Note Removing a delegate does not delete any transactions they created. Records keep their original creator attribution, and rows they entered in a joint account stay on your ledger.

If you (the owner) have 2FA enabled, the delegate must also enable 2FA on their own account before they can act as you. When a delegate tries to switch into an owner's context and the owner has 2FA but the delegate does not, the switch is blocked with: "That account requires two-factor authentication. Set up 2FA in Settings before switching." This is a non-negotiable requirement. Authenticator secrets are per-user and are never shared between the owner and the delegate -- so the delegate must independently prove possession of a second factor for their own login before they can access a 2FA-protected dataset. See Settings and Security > Two-Factor Authentication for setup details.

Delegates never see your password, your 2FA secret, your backup codes, or your trusted-device list. Changing your password does not automatically revoke active delegate sessions -- if you need to cut off a delegate, use Remove on the Shared Access page. Delegate requests are scoped by the server. Even if a delegate crafted a direct API call to an account they were not granted, the request would be rejected with a permission error. Joint access is enforced the same way. Which accounts are natively visible, which of them accept writes, whether a transfer connects and what the net worth includes are all recomputed from the live grants on every request -- the interface never gets to decide. An account shared with someone cannot be re-shared by them. Delegated accounts are absent from the Edit access dialog entirely, so sharing never chains. A request for a joint account you were not granted returns "not found" rather than "forbidden", so probing cannot confirm that an account exists. Invite links are stored only as a fingerprint, expire after 24 hours, and work once. Shared Access and emergency access are not part of a backup : restoring your data does not restore who you shared it with. Personal Access Tokens (see Settings and Security > Personal Access Tokens ) belong to the user that created them. A delegate's PAT does not grant access to the owner's data -- a delegate would need to switch context interactively and create the PAT while acting as the owner.

Emergency Access lets you designate one or more trusted contacts who will automatically receive a magic link to take over your Monize account if you do not sign in for an extended period. It is intended for incapacitation, hospitalization, or worst-case scenarios where a partner, family member, or executor needs to access your financial records on your behalf. The feature is fully automated. Once configured, a daily background check watches for inactivity and, when the threshold is reached, emails each designated contact a single-use link that lets them set a new password on your account. You are reminded by email before the grant happens, giving you a chance to sign in and reset the countdown.

Step What happens 1. You enable the feature You add one or more trusted contacts and pick two thresholds: when reminders start and when access is granted 2. You stop using Monize The server tracks the time of your last authenticated activity 3. Reminder window is reached Once per day, you receive an email warning that emergency access is approaching 4. Grant window is reached Each contact receives a single-use magic link by email; you receive no further reminders 5. A contact claims the link They set a new password, all existing sessions are revoked, and they are signed in as you 6. The feature auto-disables Emergency Access turns itself off on the now-claimed account so the cycle does not repeat If you come back before anyone claims a link, the next daily check voids the links and starts the countdown again (see What Happens When Access Is Granted ). Important Emergency Access is a "dead-man's switch", not a real-time alert. It is designed to fire only after days or weeks of inactivity. It is not the right tool for ongoing shared access -- use Shared Access for that.

Emergency Access depends on two things your administrator configures on the server: Outbound email (the SMTP_HOST , SMTP_USER , and SMTP_PASSWORD environment variables). Reminders and claim links are sent by email. ENCRYPTION_KEY . Each contact's claim link is stored encrypted so a failed delivery can be retried with the same link, and the message to your contacts is stored encrypted too. When either is missing, the Emergency Access page says so at the top ( Email is not configured or Encryption key required ), and the controls that would arm the feature -- Enable emergency access , the two day counts, Add contact and the message buttons -- are disabled. A feature that is already enabled can always be switched off, even on a server that has since lost its email settings or its key. The feature is not available: In demo mode When viewing another user's account through Shared Access (only the account owner can configure their own emergency access)

Open Settings (the gear icon with your name in the top-right corner) and choose Emergency Access in the settings menu, or click the Emergency Access card on the Settings page. The page has four cards: Settings -- the on/off switch and the two inactivity thresholds Message to your contacts -- an optional, encrypted note for your contacts Emergency Contacts -- the people who receive a claim link Status -- your last activity, the last reminder sent, and whether access has been granted

Open Settings > Emergency Access Add at least one contact (see Adding Emergency Contacts ) Turn on Enable emergency access Set the inactivity thresholds (see below ) Click Save settings Enabling the feature does not, by itself, send any emails. Reminders and grants only fire when the inactivity thresholds are exceeded. Access is never granted while you have no contacts: with an empty list the daily check simply skips you.

Emergency Access uses two day-count thresholds: Setting Default Range Description Days of inactivity before access is granted 14 2--365 After this many days without an authenticated request from you, each contact is emailed a claim link Days of inactivity before reminder emails 7 1--364 After this many days, you start receiving a once-per-day warning email Both are whole days, and the reminder threshold must be strictly less than the grant threshold (the form will reject saves that violate this).

Any authenticated request to the Monize server resets the clock -- opening the dashboard, viewing a report, recording a transaction, or an integration using one of your API tokens. You do not need to sign in fresh; an open session that quietly refreshes counts as activity. The Status card shows Last access (with how long ago it was), Last reminder sent , and Grant status ( not yet granted , or the date access was granted). If you have not been active since this feature was deployed, the server falls back to your last sign-in time.

In the Emergency Contacts card, click Add contact Enter the contact's First name and Email Click Add contact You can add as many contacts as you want, each with a different email address. Each contact receives their own magic link when access is granted -- whichever contact claims the link first wins, and the remaining contacts' links are automatically voided. You can Edit a contact's first name or email at any time. Editing the email invalidates any link that has already been issued to the old address, so you do not need to disable the feature while you make the change. You can Remove a contact from the list. Removing a contact also invalidates any link they may already be holding. A contact added after access was granted is sent a link of their own at the next daily check. Tip Use the first name only -- the email addresses the contact by first name ("Hi Alice"), so a last name is unnecessary.

You can write an optional message of up to 4,000 characters that will be included in the grant email and shown to the contact on the claim page. Typical contents: Where to find paper records, safe-deposit-box keys, or password managers Account numbers for institutions that are not in Monize Funeral wishes or instructions for executors A note explaining why they are receiving the email

The message is encrypted at rest with a server-held key, and reading or writing it requires re-verifying your identity. This protects the message from someone who has hijacked an already-open Monize session. In the Message to your contacts card, click Add message (first time) or Edit message Confirm it is you in the Confirm it's you dialog: Password users: enter your current account password Two-factor users: enter the 6-digit code from your authenticator app Single sign-on users: continue to your identity provider to sign in again Type the message and click Save message After verification, the message is unlocked for five minutes -- an Unlocked for MM:SS countdown displays in the message card. Click Lock now to re-lock immediately. Once locked, you must re-verify to view or edit it again. Saving an empty message removes it.

While locked, the message card shows whether a message is set, its character count, and the last time it was updated -- but the content stays hidden until you click Reveal message and re-verify. Note The message is stored encrypted with AES-256-GCM under the server's ENCRYPTION_KEY , so a copy of the database alone does not reveal it. The running server holds the key and decrypts the message when including it in a grant email or showing it to you after you re-verify.

Once you cross the reminder threshold, Monize sends you a reminder email from its daily check, which runs at 9:00 AM server time. The email tells you: How many days you have been inactive How many days remain until access is granted Which contacts will be notified At most one reminder is sent per day. Using Monize again resets the counter and stops the reminders. If outbound email or ENCRYPTION_KEY is not configured on the server, no reminders are sent and no access is granted. The Emergency Access page displays a warning when this is the case.

h: What Happens When Access Is Granted
x: When the grant threshold is reached: A single-use claim link is generated for each contact Each contact receives an email titled "You have been granted emergency access to [Your Name] 's Monize account" The link is valid for 30 days The page displays a red banner the next time you sign in: "Emergency access already granted" , with the date it happened If you come back before anyone claims a link , the next daily check notices that you are active again: it voids every outstanding link, resets the countdown and emails you to say so. A link cannot be claimed once you are back within the grant window, even before that check has run. To void the links straight away instead, clear the granted state (see Clearing the Granted State ). If a link could not be delivered to a contact (for example, the email server was briefly unavailable), the daily check sends that contact the same link again.

If you have received an emergency access email, follow these steps to take over the account: Open the link in the email. It looks like https://your-monize-server/emergency-access/claim?token=... The page greets you by name, names the account holder, and shows their message if they wrote one Enter a New Password (it must meet Monize's standard requirements and must not appear in the Have I Been Pwned breach database) Enter it again in Confirm Password and click Claim emergency access After a successful claim: The owner's previous password is replaced by yours All existing sessions are signed out, and the account's trusted devices, personal access tokens and connected AI or MCP client authorizations are revoked Two-factor authentication is disabled on the account (you will need to re-enable it under Settings if you want it) All sibling magic links for the same account are voided -- you are the sole new holder Emergency Access is automatically disabled on the now-claimed account You are signed in and taken to the dashboard Important One-shot only. The claim link can be used only once. Refreshing the page after a successful claim, or opening it from a second browser, fails with "This emergency access link is invalid, expired, or has already been used."
The claim page's requests (showing the preview and completing the claim) are limited to 5 attempts per 15 minutes per IP address, so a brute-force search for valid links is infeasible.

If a grant fires by accident (e.g., you were on vacation and ignored the reminder emails), you can void all outstanding claim links once you sign back in: Open Settings > Emergency Access A red banner reads "Emergency access already granted" Click Clear granted state Confirm with Clear in the dialog Clearing the granted state: Voids every outstanding magic link for your contacts Resets the grant marker and the reminder schedule, so the next cycle starts fresh from your current activity Leaves the feature enabled (so reminders will resume if you go inactive again) If you want to switch it off entirely, disable the feature instead (see below).

Open Settings > Emergency Access Turn off Enable emergency access Click Save settings Disabling the feature: Stops the daily check for your account immediately Voids any outstanding magic links Keeps your contact list and message intact, so you can re-enable later without re-entering them To remove the message or contacts permanently, edit them individually.

Concern Mitigation Database leak of the message The message body is encrypted at rest with AES-256-GCM keyed by the server's ENCRYPTION_KEY Claim link leak from the database A link only works with its random token, and the database holds the token's hash plus a copy encrypted under ENCRYPTION_KEY -- never the token in the clear Brute-forcing claim links 256-bit random tokens; a limit of 5 requests per 15 minutes per IP address on both preview and claim Link reuse / replay Single-use: the claim consumes the link and voids every sibling link for the same owner in the same database transaction Stale links after the owner returns Links stop working as soon as the owner is active again, the daily check voids them, and disabling or clearing the granted state voids them immediately. Links also expire after 30 days Stale session reading the message Reading or writing the message requires re-proving your identity within the last five minutes Account hijack via emergency access Access is only granted after the configured number of consecutive inactive days. Any authenticated request resets the counter

Email delivery is critical. If you change your email provider or your contact changes theirs, the grant email may bounce silently. Keep the contact list current. The clock is server-side. An open Monize tab that quietly refreshes its session counts as activity -- close the tab if you genuinely want the timer to advance. The first claim wins. If you have multiple contacts, they cannot share access through this feature -- the first to claim takes over the account, and the others are locked out. Use Shared Access if you want multiple people to have ongoing access. Two-factor authentication is disabled on claim. The new account holder can re-enable it from Settings, but there is a brief window where the account has only password protection. Single sign-on accounts become password accounts on claim. Because the claim sets a password, the account signs in with that password from then on. If the contact wants to keep using SSO afterward, an administrator would need to re-link the account. Not part of a backup. Emergency access settings, contacts and the message are not included in backups ; after restoring onto a new server, set them up again.

Monize includes a full backup and restore system to protect your financial data. You can download a backup on demand, restore from any backup file, take and restore the automatic backups the server keeps for you, and send copies of those off the server. An administrator sets the schedule and retention of the automatic backups for the whole deployment. Backups are encrypted by default. If you sign in with an email and password, every backup Monize writes is encrypted with that password -- there is nothing to switch on, and nothing extra to remember. That also means a backup file is only as recoverable as the password it was written under, so read Passwords, Keys, and What You Must Not Lose before you rely on these files. Everything for your own backups is in Settings > Backup & Restore : open Settings (the gear icon with your name in the top-right corner) and choose Backup & Restore in the settings menu.

You can download a full backup of your data at any time. Open Settings > Backup & Restore Under Create Backup , click Download Backup In the Encrypt Backup dialog, enter the password to encrypt the file with -- your login password (or your backup password, if you sign in with SSO) Click Download Your browser downloads a file named monize-backup-YYYY-MM-DD.mzbe , dated in your own time zone Warning The file is encrypted with exactly what you type in that dialog. Monize does not check it against your login password, so a typo produces a file that only the mistyped password opens. Type carefully, or use a password manager. If your backups are not encrypted (an SSO account that has set no backup password), there is no dialog and the file is named monize-backup-YYYY-MM-DD.json.gz instead. The backup contains all of your financial data, including the files attached to your transactions, as gzip-compressed JSON, wrapped in an encrypted envelope when encryption is on. It is streamed from the server, so a large dataset does not have to fit in memory. If some attachment files could not be read intact, the download still completes but you are told the backup is incomplete and how many attachments are missing or failed their integrity check. Do not treat such a file as a full backup: fix the attachment storage and export again.

Restoring replaces all of your existing data with the contents of the backup file. This is useful for recovering from data loss, migrating to a new server, or reverting after an unwanted change. Caution Restoring a backup permanently replaces all of your current data. This operation cannot be undone. Consider downloading a backup of your current data first.

Open Settings > Backup & Restore Under Restore from Backup , click Restore from Backup... Read the warning, then use Select backup file to pick a backup ( .mzbe , .json.gz , .gz or .json ) If the file is encrypted, a Backup password field appears: enter the password the backup was created with. You can leave it empty to try your current password first. Enter your account password to confirm (SSO accounts click Re-authenticate and Restore instead, sign in again with their identity provider, and pick the file again when they come back) Click Confirm Restore You can also restore one of the automatic backups the server keeps for you : its Restore button puts that file into this same form. After a successful restore, a Restore Complete dialog lists the number of records restored for each kind of data and the total. It also names anything that could not be brought back as it was: Attachments whose files the backup did not carry intact (export a fresh backup once attachment storage is healthy) AI providers restored without a usable API key (enter the key again in Settings > AI Settings ) Government bond holdings that could not be linked to their bond on this server, or whose series could not be fetched from the official source, with what to do for each

A restore is all-or-nothing: Checks first. The file is decrypted, decompressed and validated, your password is checked, and attachment files are prepared, before anything is deleted. A file that is too large for this server, damaged, or written by a newer version of Monize than this one, and a server whose database is missing an update, are refused at this point, with a message saying why and leaving your data untouched. Replace. In one database transaction, all of your existing data is removed and the backup's data is inserted in dependency order, with links between records (parent categories, linked accounts, transfers and so on) reconnected at the end. Commit. If any step fails, the entire transaction is rolled back and no data is changed. If the connection drops before the server answers, Monize tells you so: reload the page to see whether the restore applied before trying again. A restore that was interrupted by a server restart can be retried after about 15 minutes, and the message says how long to wait. The largest backup a server accepts for restore depends on how much memory the server has; an administrator can adjust the limits. A file over the limit is refused before anything changes.

h: Passwords, Keys, and What You Must Not Lose
x: Encrypted backups protect your data from anyone who gets hold of the file. The same property is what makes them unrecoverable if you lose what opens them, and Monize has no master override -- the server genuinely cannot read a backup without the password it was written under. There are two separate secrets, they do different jobs, and losing them has different consequences. Both are worth writing down somewhere durable.

h: 1. The password a backup was written with (you)
x: A backup file opens with the password that was in effect when that file was written -- not your current one. If you sign in with an email and password , that is your login password on the day of the backup (or, for a manual download, the password you typed in the Encrypt Backup dialog). Change your password, and every backup taken before the change still needs the old one. Restoring a recent backup usually asks nothing extra, but a six-month-old file taken before a password change will ask -- and only the old password will do. If you sign in with SSO , it is the backup password you set in Settings, as it was at the time of writing. Changing it later does not re-encrypt anything already on disk. Important Before you change your password, ask what would open your oldest backup. The safest habit is to keep every backup password you have ever used in a password manager, dated. The second safest is to download a fresh backup immediately after changing your password, and treat the older files as needing the old one.

ENCRYPTION_KEY is a server setting, not something you type. It encrypts what the database holds: your AI provider API keys, your Google Places API key for payee lookup , emergency-access links and messages, mailbox, bank sync and off-site storage credentials, the instance's browser-push key pair, and the server's copy of each user's backup key -- which is what lets scheduled backups run encrypted without prompting you every night. If it is not set, your automatic backups are not encrypted. Monize still starts -- and says so loudly in its startup log every time, including that a future release will refuse to start without it -- but until an administrator sets it, there is nowhere to keep the backup key those backups would be encrypted with. If your backup files are .json.gz rather than .mzbe , this is usually why. Keep it safe, and keep it the same. Store it with your other deployment secrets -- the same place you keep JWT_SECRET and your database password. Changing it does not re-encrypt anything; it simply makes what is already stored unreadable. If ENCRYPTION_KEY is lost or changed: What happens What it takes to recover Automatic backups stop , reporting an error rather than quietly writing unencrypted files (this is the changed case; a key that was never set at all just produces unencrypted backups) Each user signs in again (or confirms their password in Settings > Backup & Restore ), which stores a fresh backup key Stored AI provider API keys become unreadable Re-enter them in Settings > AI Settings A stored Google Places API key becomes unreadable Re-enter it in Settings > Payee Lookup Emergency-access links and messages become unreadable Re-configure emergency access Stored mailbox, bank sync and off-site bucket credentials become unreadable Connect them again The instance's browser-push key pair becomes unreadable, so no push notification can be delivered An admin rotates the key pair in Admin > Notifications ; every device registers again Your existing backup files are unaffected Nothing -- they open with the password they were written under, exactly as before That last row is the one people get wrong in both directions. ENCRYPTION_KEY does not unlock a backup file, so losing it does not strand your backups; and having it does not rescue a backup whose password you have forgotten. Note Upgrading from an older version? This setting used to be called AI_ENCRYPTION_KEY and was documented as being for AI providers only. The old name still works and still takes precedence, so an existing deployment needs no changes. If you never set it, your automatic backups were -- and still are -- being written unencrypted : set ENCRYPTION_KEY ( openssl rand -hex 32 ), restart, and sign in once so Monize can make your backup key. Backups written from then on will be .mzbe .

An unencrypted backup is a gzip-compressed JSON file -- anyone who obtains it (intercepted in transit, copied from a cloud-sync folder, recovered from an old drive) can read every transaction, payee, and account name, and the API keys of your AI providers. Encryption wraps the backup in a password-protected envelope so the contents stay confidential even if the file leaks. Both manual downloads and scheduled automatic backups are encrypted whenever Monize has a usable backup key for your account, which for a password account is all the time.

Encryption is the default rather than an option because a backup is the one file that contains everything, and it is the file most likely to end up somewhere you did not plan: Backups folders get synced to cloud storage (Dropbox, OneDrive, Google Drive, Backblaze) Backups get emailed, copied to a NAS, or uploaded to remote storage Servers, volumes, and external drives get shared, sold, or stolen The cost of that default is the thing to be deliberate about: an encrypted backup is exactly as recoverable as the password it was written with. See Passwords, Keys, and What You Must Not Lose .

If you sign in with an email and password (the default), your backups are encrypted with that password automatically. There is no separate password to invent, and nothing to switch on. Monize never stores your password. At the only moments it sees it -- when you register, sign in, or change it -- it creates a random backup key and keeps two copies of it: one locked with your password, which goes into the header of every automatic backup so your password opens the file, and one locked with the server's ENCRYPTION_KEY , so the nightly job can encrypt without asking you. Each password change makes a new key, so an old password never opens a backup written after the change. Settings > Backup & Restore shows the state under Backup Encryption : What you see What it means Enabled -- "Backups are encrypted with your login password." Nothing to do. Not enabled , with an Enable with My Login Password button Monize has no backup key for you yet -- usually because you have stayed signed in since before this feature existed. Click the button and confirm your login password in the Enable Encrypted Backups dialog; backups from then on are encrypted. Signing out and back in does the same thing. "This server is not configured to encrypt backups, so they are written unencrypted." The server has no ENCRYPTION_KEY , so your automatic backups are being written unencrypted . That is a deployment setting an administrator has to fix -- see ENCRYPTION_KEY . There is no Disable button for a password account: your backup key is remade every time you sign in, so turning encryption off would last until your next sign-in. When you change your login password, a new key is made automatically -- but files already on disk keep needing the password they were written with.

h: Setting a Backup Password (OIDC / SSO Users)
x: If your account uses Single Sign-On (OIDC) , there is no login password to reuse. You set a dedicated backup password instead. Open Settings > Backup & Restore In the Backup Encryption section, click Set Backup Password Enter a new backup password (at least 12 characters, and not in the Have I Been Pwned breach database) Click Confirm The backup password is independent from your SSO credentials -- you choose and manage it yourself. Save it somewhere secure (a password manager is ideal); without it, encrypted backups cannot be restored. To change it later, click Change Backup Password and repeat the process. The new password takes effect for backups written from that point on; previously-written backups remain decryptable only with the password that was active when they were created.

See Manual Backup : with encryption on, Download Backup first asks for the password in the Encrypt Backup dialog. The .mzbe extension (Monize Backup Encrypted) distinguishes encrypted backups from the unencrypted .json.gz format. The password is sent over HTTPS in a request header and is never written to access logs.

The restore form accepts both unencrypted ( .json , .json.gz , .gz ) and encrypted ( .mzbe ) files, and recognises an encrypted file as soon as you pick it: the form then shows "This backup is encrypted. Enter the backup password it was created with:" above the account password. Monize tries, in order, the backup password you entered, your account password, and the backup key it holds for you (which opens your automatic backups). If none of them opens the file -- typically because it was created when you had a different password -- you are asked to enter the password it was created with in the Backup password field and try again. This handles cases where you have changed your password since the backup, or are restoring a very old backup onto a fresh install. Warning If you have lost the password, an encrypted backup cannot be recovered. Monize has no master override -- by design, the server cannot decrypt the file without the password. Always keep a copy of your backup password in a password manager.

h: Changing or Disabling the Backup Password
x: Local users: changing your login password automatically makes a new backup key, so backups written from then on use the new password. Files already written still need the password that was active when they were created -- keep it. There is no way to turn encryption off for a password account. OIDC users: click Change Backup Password to set a new one, or Disable to turn encryption off entirely. As with local users, existing encrypted backups still require whichever password was active when they were written.

Detail Value Cipher AES-256-GCM (authenticated encryption) Key derivation scrypt (N=32768, r=8, p=1) from the password, with a random salt per file Integrity Every part of the file is authenticated, so a wrong password, truncation, bit-flips or a swapped header are all detected and the restore fails safely Automatic backups Encrypted with your random backup key; the key, locked with your password, travels in the file's header An encrypted backup starts with the four ASCII characters MZBE , which is how Monize (and you) can tell one apart from a plain gzip file.

Monize can automatically back up every account's data on a schedule, writing a compressed (and, normally, encrypted) backup file per account to the server's backup storage. Automatic backup is a deployment concern, so it is configured by an administrator on Admin > Backups , and the schedule and retention set there apply to every active account on the deployment. Everyone else has nothing to set up: they can download or restore the files kept for them (see Automatic Backups Kept for You ) and choose off-site copies of their own. Note An automatic backup is not a full database backup. It holds each account's own financial records, in the same format as a manual download, and nothing else: no database schema, no server configuration, no other deployment's data. For whole-instance disaster recovery, back up the PostgreSQL database and the attachment storage with your own tools.

Open Admin > Backups (admin role required) Turn on Enable automatic backups Configure the folder, frequency, time and retention Click Save Policy Saving applies the policy to every account at once. A line under the description says how far it reaches: "Scheduled on N of M active accounts on this deployment."

The Backup Storage line shows where backups go, chosen by the server's BACKUP_STORAGE_PROVIDER setting: a Local folder (the default) or S3-compatible object storage . It also says how many backup files the store currently holds for your own account. Switching storage does not move existing backups. With a local folder, the Backup Folder must be an absolute path inside a directory the server allows ( /data/backups by default; see Docker Volume Configuration ): Use Browse... to navigate the server's backup directories and click Select This Folder Click Validate to confirm the folder exists and is writable Each account's backups go into a folder of their own inside it, named for the account's ID; the page shows an example path With S3 storage there is no folder to choose: the bucket and key prefix are the deployment's, and each account's backups go under their own key prefix. If the configured storage cannot be written to, the page says "This deployment has no backup storage" before you set a schedule, rather than after the first failed run. Note The folder must be writable by the backend process. In Docker deployments, you must map a host directory to the container path using a volume mount.

Frequency Description Every 6 Hours Backs up 4 times per day, starting at the configured backup time Every 12 Hours Backs up twice per day, starting at the configured backup time Daily Backs up once per day at the configured time Weekly Backs up once per week at the configured time Set the Backup Time to control when backups run (24-hour format, e.g., 02:00 for 2 AM). The label shows the time zone it is interpreted in, which is the administrator's own time-zone preference. Backups start on the hour, so the minutes are not used.

Monize uses a three-tier retention system to balance storage usage with backup history: Tier Default Range Description Daily backups 7 0--365 The most recent days' backups to keep Weekly backups 4 0--52 Weekly copies to keep Monthly backups 6 0--120 Monthly copies to keep Each run writes that day's daily backup. There is one daily file per day: with a 6- or 12-hour frequency, a later run the same day replaces the earlier file. On the 7th, 14th, 21st and 28th of the month, the day's backup is also kept as a weekly copy. On the 1st of the month, the day's backup is also kept as a monthly copy. After each run, the oldest files beyond each tier's count are deleted. A backup that could not include every attachment is saved as a separate partial file instead of a daily one, so it never takes the place of a complete backup. Partial files are kept to the same count as daily ones. Backup files are named by their retention tier and the date (in the policy's time zone): Tier File Name Pattern Daily monize-backup-daily-YYYY-MM-DD.mzbe Weekly monize-backup-weekly-YYYY-MM-DD.mzbe Monthly monize-backup-monthly-YY-MM.mzbe Partial monize-backup-partial-YYYY-MM-DD.mzbe An account whose backups are not encrypted gets .json.gz instead of .mzbe . Retention recognises both extensions, so unencrypted backups from before encryption was turned on are still managed correctly. Files that do not follow these names -- including backups an older version wrote directly into the base folder -- are never deleted by retention; remove those by hand once you no longer need them. Note If the server cannot use an account's stored backup key -- typically because ENCRYPTION_KEY changed -- that account's scheduled backup fails rather than silently writing an unencrypted file. The person signs in again (or confirms their password in Settings > Backup & Restore ) to store a fresh key. A backup that goes out unencrypted for any other reason is recorded as a warning in the server log.

Click Back Up Every Account Now to back up every active account immediately, outside the regular schedule. The files are written to the same storage and follow the same retention rules; the regular schedule is not moved. When it finishes, a message says how many accounts were backed up, and how many were partial or failed.

Once backups have run, the page shows a Deployment Status box: Field Description Most recent backup Date and time of the latest backup of any account, with its result: Success , Partial or Failed Error The error message, if the latest backup failed Next scheduled backup When the next automatic backup of any account is due A failed or partial backup also raises an alert in the administrators' notification bell.

When automatic backups run on your server, Settings > Backup & Restore has a folded Automatic Backups list of the files the server holds for your own account. Click the heading to open it. Each file shows its name, Date Modified and Size , with two buttons: Download saves a copy to your device Restore puts that file into the restore form above, so it goes through the same password prompt, warning, confirmation and summary as a file picked from disk (see How to Restore ) The list is absent on a server that runs no automatic backups. It stays while a switched-off schedule's files are still there to recover, and says so if it cannot be loaded rather than looking empty. Administrators also see a link to Admin > Backups here.

A backup that lives only on the server is lost with the server. Under Off-site destinations inside the Automatic Backups list, you can have an encrypted copy of each complete automatic backup sent elsewhere -- three copies, two kinds of storage, one of them off the machine: S3 storage -- set Copy Destination to Off , This server's bucket (when the administrator has configured one) or My own bucket . For your own bucket, enter the Bucket , Region , an optional Key prefix , an Endpoint for an S3-compatible service such as MinIO, R2 or B2 (with Use path-style addressing where it needs it), and an Access key ID and Secret access key . The keys are stored encrypted and never shown again; Remove Stored Credentials forgets them. Email -- turn on Email me a copy of each completed automatic backup and enter the address in Send copies to . A backup larger than the server's email size limit is not attached; you receive a notice naming the file instead. Click Save Destinations to keep the settings. Only an encrypted backup ever leaves the server: an unencrypted one is skipped and an administrator is alerted. A copy sent to a bucket is only ever added, never overwritten or deleted by Monize, so ageing old copies out is up to the bucket's own lifecycle rules. Each backup in the list shows a small icon per destination with the copy's state (for example Copied , Sending , Failed or Skipped: not encrypted ); a failed copy is retried automatically.

A backup includes all of your own data: Category Data Included Preferences User preferences, currency preferences, notification preferences, reminders and notifications Accounts All account types and their settings, and financial institutions Transactions Transactions, splits, tags, and attachments including the files themselves Scheduled Transactions Recurring bills/deposits, splits, overrides, postings and payroll deduction rules Categories & Payees Category hierarchy, payees, and payee aliases Tags All tags and tag assignments Rules Transaction rules Calendar Day notes Loans Loan/mortgage interest-rate change history and saved overpayment scenarios Investments Securities, security prices and documents, security tags, holdings, investment transactions, and the identity of any government bond series you hold Budgets Budgets, budget categories, budget periods, and budget alerts Reports Custom report definitions, investment reports, retirement (Monte Carlo) scenarios and GEM strategies Warranties Warranties and their claims Email Receipts The parsers (profiles) that read your receipts AI and Payee Lookup AI provider settings with their API keys, and payee lookup settings with its key Import Settings Saved column mapping presets Currencies The definition of every currency your data uses Net Worth History Monthly account balance snapshots Automatic Backup Your automatic backup settings (the deployment's policy itself is not in anyone's backup) API keys are stored encrypted with the server's ENCRYPTION_KEY , which cannot travel with the file, so a backup carries them decrypted and the restoring server encrypts them again under its own key. That is one more reason to keep backups encrypted. Not included: your login itself (password, two-factor secrets, trusted devices, sessions and personal access tokens), the people you share with and your emergency access settings, connected mailboxes and the emails received from them, bank sync connections, the shared market exchange rates, the undo history, and caches Monize can rebuild. After restoring on a new server, sign in with your existing credentials and set those up again.

h: Support Backup (Share a Bug Report Safely)
x: When you hit a bug that is hard to describe, a support backup lets you attach real-looking data to a GitHub issue without sharing your actual finances . Open Settings > Help & Support and click Create a support backup . A support backup is an ordinary backup file that restores through the normal flow into a throwaway instance -- there is nothing new to install to open it -- but it is de-identified first: Names are masked , keeping the first and last two characters ( Biedronka becomes Bi*****ka ), and free text and secrets are dropped -- descriptions, notes, memos, reference and account numbers, and API keys. Your amounts are scaled by a single hidden multiplier, while public values that would give the multiplier away -- exchange rates, security prices, interest rates -- are kept intact. Balances and split totals are recomputed so everything still adds up. Every ID is replaced , so the file cannot be correlated back to your account or to another support backup. Currencies you created yourself get a random code and a masked name. The de-identification works from a strict allowlist , so a future database column cannot silently start leaking. The dialog lets you shape the file: Option What it does Sections to Include Investments, scheduled transactions, budgets, reports and projections, import column mappings, and auto-backup settings, each on or off Include security price history Off by default: a full price series matches public market data and can identify a masked ticker. Turn it on only when the bug concerns prices or valuations. Limit to specific accounts Leave all unchecked to include every account. Picking some also brings in the accounts and payees they refer to. Date range (optional) Trims history outside the dates; opening balances are adjusted so the trimmed file still reconciles Amount multiplier The hidden factor, any non-integer greater than 1. Regenerate picks a new one. Never share it. Encryption password Pre-filled with a random password (at least 8 characters). The file is always encrypted. Share this password with the investigator through a separate channel, not alongside the file. Click Preview to see a before-and-after sample of what the de-identification does to your rows, then Generate . Monize asks you to confirm you saved the password ( I saved it -- generate ), because it is not stored anywhere and cannot be recovered later. Important This is de-identification, not anonymity. Dates, frequencies, and structure survive on purpose so bugs still reproduce -- it protects against casual exposure, not against someone who already knows you. Do not treat a support backup as fully anonymous, and do not share the multiplier.

Inside the encryption (or directly, for an unencrypted backup), a backup is a gzip-compressed JSON document with the following structure: { "version": 1, "exportedAt": "2026-04-03T02:00:00.000Z", "currencies": [...], "user_preferences": [...], "accounts": [...], "transactions": [...], ... } version -- Backup format version (currently 1 ) exportedAt -- ISO 8601 timestamp of when the backup was created Each table is represented as an array of row objects; attachment files travel base64-encoded with a size and SHA-256 checksum that are verified when the backup is written and again when it is restored A backup restores onto the same or a newer version of Monize. A backup taken under one attachment storage (database, local disk or S3) restores under another.

When running Monize in Docker, the backend container runs with a read-only filesystem for security, so automatic backups need a host directory mapped into the container. The supplied docker-compose files already do this: BACKUP_HOST_DIR (default ./monize/backups ) is mapped to BACKUP_CONTAINER_DIR (default /data/backups ) inside the backend container: services: backend: # ... existing configuration ... volumes: - ${BACKUP_HOST_DIR:-./monize/backups}:${BACKUP_CONTAINER_DIR:-/data/backups} Then use /data/backups (or a folder inside it) as the backup folder on Admin > Backups . Folders outside BACKUP_CONTAINER_DIR are refused unless they are listed in the server's BACKUP_ALLOWED_ROOTS setting. Tip Choose a host path that is included in your server's own backup strategy (e.g., a path covered by your NAS snapshots or cloud sync) for an extra layer of protection.

Backup and restore operations include several security measures: Measure Description Authentication All backup operations require a valid login session; the automatic backup policy is admin-only Restore verification Restoring requires password re-entry or a fresh SSO sign-in File encryption by default Backups are wrapped in an AES-256-GCM envelope keyed by your own password whenever the server holds a usable backup key for you -- automatic for password accounts (see Encrypted Backups ) Server-side key The server's copy of each backup key, AI provider keys, the Google Places key, emergency-access links, stored credentials and the browser-push key pair are encrypted with ENCRYPTION_KEY . Without it nothing can be stored encrypted and automatic backups go out in the clear; the server warns at every start and a future release will require it User isolation Backups only contain data belonging to the authenticated user, and each account's automatic backups live in their own folder or key prefix Validated restore Only known data tables and columns are restored, every value goes through parameterized queries, and every reference inside the file must point to a row of the same file Size limits Restore uploads are limited to what the server's memory can safely process; larger files are refused before anything changes Confined folders Automatic backup folders must sit inside the directories the server allows, and paths are checked so they cannot lead outside them Transaction safety Restore runs in one database transaction with full rollback on error Off-site copies Only encrypted backups are sent off the server, and copies in a bucket are never overwritten or deleted by Monize Demo restrictions Downloads, restores, off-site destinations and the automatic backup policy are disabled in demo mode, with a note on the page saying why

Download a backup before major changes -- Before bulk-deleting data, re-importing, or updating Monize, download a manual backup first Test your backups -- Periodically verify that a backup can be restored successfully by restoring on a test instance Use auto-backup with retention -- Administrators should enable automatic backups on Admin > Backups with the default retention settings (7 daily, 4 weekly, 6 monthly) for comprehensive coverage without excessive storage use Send a copy off the server -- Turn on an off-site destination so losing the server's disk does not mean losing every backup Check that your backups actually are encrypted -- Look at Settings > Backup & Restore : it should say Enabled , and your backup files should end in .mzbe . A .json.gz file is readable by anyone who has it Save every backup password you have used, dated -- A backup opens with the password in effect when it was written, not your current one. A lost password means a lost backup: there is no master override. See Passwords, Keys, and What You Must Not Lose Back up ENCRYPTION_KEY with your other deployment secrets -- If you run the server, store it wherever you keep JWT_SECRET and your database password. Losing it does not lock you out of your backup files , but it does make every stored API key and credential unreadable and stops automatic backups until each user signs in again Map the backup volume to durable storage -- Point your Docker volume at a path that is covered by your server's own backup or sync strategy Keep off-site copies -- Periodically download a manual backup and store it separately from your server (e.g., cloud storage or external drive) for disaster recovery Set a quiet backup time -- Schedule auto-backups during off-peak hours (e.g., 2:00 AM) to minimize any performance impact
